h1:
Wat Phra Kaew Don Tao Suchadaram
Golden Chedi & Burmese Mondop in Central Lampang
intro: If you had to pick one temple that tells the full story of Lampang, a lot of people would point to Wat Phra Kaew Don Tao Suchadaram, an old temple on the bank of the Wang River that housed the Emerald Buddha for several decades. You get a Lanna-style golden chedi, a teak Mandalay-Burmese mondop so pretty that people can't stop photographing it, and the legend of Lady Suchada that gave the temple its name. You can walk the whole thing in an hour, but you come away with both the history and some great photo angles.
chips: 🛕 Old temple in the old town

blocks.html: Wat Phra Kaew Don Tao Suchadaram is a royal temple sitting on the Wiang Nuea side of Lampang, on a small rise by the Wang River. Locals treat it as one of the city's sacred temples, while visitors from elsewhere usually know it for two things: it was the former home of the Emerald Buddha before the image moved on to Bangkok, and the teak Burmese-style mondop that stands out in the middle of the temple grounds. The real draw here is the atmosphere — come early when there are still few people and the slanting sun lands right on the golden chedi, and you can wander and shoot at an easy pace.

blocks.text: The Golden Chedi — Phra Borommathat Don Tao

blocks.html: The temple's main feature is the large chedi people call Phra Borommathat Don Tao — a white square base rising into a bell that's clad in gleaming brass top to bottom. It's believed to enshrine a hair relic of the Buddha. The chedi stands roughly 50 metres tall and is the oldest Lanna-style work in the temple, dating back to around the 14th–15th century. When the sun hits it, the gold catches the light from a distance, and it's a landmark that drivers coming into Lampang look out for.

items: The white square base plays off the gold-clad bell — the best angle is standing diagonally so you catch the base and the spire together.
Walking clockwise (pradakshina) around the chedi is a custom worshippers do three times.
Late afternoon with soft light turns the gold warm-toned, and shots against the sky come out nicer than at midday.

blocks.text: The Teak Burmese Mondop — The Highlight People Come For

blocks.html: The other spot you shouldn't skip is the Burmese-style mondop, built in 1909 (B.E. 2452) by a wealthy Burmese trader who came in during Lampang's teak-logging boom. The whole structure is teak, topped with a seven-tiered prasat-style Burmese roof (pyatthat), decorated with coloured glass and fine fretwork. Inside sits a Mandalay-style Buddha image — genuine Burmese craftsmanship that you don't often get to see in Thailand. Locals call it the finest Burmese mondop in the province.

blocks.title: Before You Enter the Mondop
blocks.html: Take off your shoes before going up, and dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered. If you've come in shorts or a strappy top, the temple usually has sarongs to borrow near the entrance. The light inside is fairly low — if you want to capture the coloured-glass detail, turn off the flash and switch to night mode for truer colours.

blocks.text: The Legend of the Emerald Buddha and Lady Suchada

blocks.html: The temple's name comes from an old legend passed down over generations. A woman named Lady Suchada is said to have found an emerald inside a watermelon (mak tao), which she offered to a senior monk. He had a craftsman carve it into a Buddha image — the source of the name Don Tao. The Suchadaram part comes from her home, which later grew into the adjoining temple. More significant than that: this temple once enshrined the Phra Phuttha Maha Mani Rattana Patimakon, or the Emerald Buddha, for about 32 years during the 14th–15th century, before it was moved on elsewhere and finally enshrined in Bangkok. Walking the temple grounds and thinking that the Emerald Buddha was once right here gives the place a different feel.

blocks.text: The Museum and Viharns Within the Temple

blocks.html: The temple grounds have other buildings worth a look — the main viharn, the Reclining Buddha viharn, and the Lanna Museum, which holds plenty of old objects, household items, Buddha images, and Lanna artefacts. You can see it all in a single loop. If you have time to spare, the adjoining Wat Suchadaram is included on the same ticket.

items.name: Reclining Buddha Viharn
items.blurb: A large reclining Buddha in a quiet, calm setting — a good spot to sit and settle before walking on.

items.name: Lanna Museum
items.blurb: A collection of old objects, household items, and Lanna artefacts that tell the story of old Lampang.

items.name: Wat Suchadaram
items.blurb: The adjoining temple, included on the same ticket — quieter and with fewer people than the chedi side.

blocks.text: Opening Hours, Entry Fee, and Getting There

items: Opening hours daily, roughly 06:00–18:00 (some parts like the museum may close earlier, around 3–5 pm).
Entry fee free for Thais, around 20 THB for foreigners (one ticket covers both the Don Tao and Suchadaram sides).
Location Phra Kaew Road, Wiang Nuea sub-district, Mueang Lampang, on the north bank of the Wang River.
Getting there from central Lampang it's about a 5–10 minute drive or horse-cart ride, with a car park inside the temple.
Time needed about 45 minutes to 1 hour to see it all.

blocks.title: The Best Time to Visit
blocks.html: Come in the morning, 7–9 am, when the air is still cool, the sun isn't harsh, and there are fewer people than later in the day. If you like warm light, late afternoon before closing is lovely in a different way. Skip midday — the temple grounds are wide open, the heat is strong, and photos are hard to get.

blocks.text: Where to Go Next, All in One Day

blocks.html: The upside of this temple is that it's right in town, so it's easy to keep going afterwards. Once you've finished, try planning the rest of the day like this.

items.activity: Start at Wat Phra Kaew Don Tao Suchadaram
items.note: Few people, with the slanting sun lighting the golden chedi

items.activity: Drive or take a horse cart into the old town for breakfast
items.note: Rice porridge, khao soi, or an old-school noodle shop

items.activity: Stop at a café in the Wang riverside area
items.note: Sip a coffee and look out over the river before noon

items.activity: Stroll Kad Kong Ta, the walking street by the Wang River
items.note: Open Sat–Sun, with century-old buildings and tons of food

items.activity: Grab an evening bite from the market stalls
items.note: Local snacks, fried treats, and northern sweets

items.activity: Walk and photograph the old buildings once the lights come on
items.note: The vintage atmosphere is clearest after dark

blocks.text: A Few Small Points of Temple Etiquette

items: Dress modestly, shoulders and knees covered, especially when entering the mondop and viharns.
Take off your shoes before going up any building, and place them neatly.
Keep your voice down and don't take selfies with your back to the main Buddha image — it's an etiquette point locals take seriously.
There are donation boxes for the temple — give as you see fit to help keep these historic sites standing.

faq.q: What are the opening hours and entry fee for Wat Phra Kaew Don Tao Suchadaram?
faq.a: It's open daily, roughly 06:00–18:00. Thais enter free, foreigners pay around 20 THB, and one ticket covers both the Don Tao side and the adjoining Wat Suchadaram. The museum may close earlier in the afternoon.

faq.q: What are the must-see highlights inside the temple?
faq.a: The golden Phra Borommathat Don Tao chedi — white base, gold spire, around 50 metres tall — the teak Mandalay-Burmese mondop with its seven-tiered roof, and the Reclining Buddha viharn, plus the Lanna Museum that holds many old Lanna pieces.

faq.q: Why is this temple connected to the Emerald Buddha?
faq.a: The temple once enshrined the Emerald Buddha for about 32 years during the 14th–15th century, before it was moved on elsewhere and finally enshrined in Bangkok. The temple's name comes from the legend of Lady Suchada, who found an emerald inside a watermelon.

faq.q: Is the temple far from central Lampang, and how do you get there?
faq.a: It's not far — it's on the Wiang Nuea side by the Wang River, only about 5–10 minutes from the city centre by car or horse cart, with a car park inside. Seeing it all takes about an hour.

faq.q: What time of day is best to visit?
faq.a: Morning, 7–9 am, is best — cool air, fewer people, and the slanting sun lighting the golden chedi. Late afternoon before closing, when the light turns warm, is also good. Avoid midday, since the temple grounds are open and exposed, the heat is strong, and photos are hard.
